question.text: What four traits of a good driver does the guide list?

answer.text: The guide lists four traits of a good driver: mindful of yourself and others, responsible for the rules of the road, familiar with how your vehicle works and takes up space, and patient and levelheaded.

teaching.text: A good driver is mindful, responsible for the rules, familiar with the vehicle, and patient and levelheaded. Remember: mindful, responsible, familiar, patient.

audio_scripts.must_match_card_back: The guide lists four traits of a good driver: mindful of yourself and others, responsible for the rules of the road, familiar with how your vehicle works and takes up space, and patient and levelheaded.

question.text: Why practice driving with intent?

answer.text: Practice with intent so that safe habits, such as looking over your shoulder to check blind zones, become automatic and free your attention for the changing road.

teaching.text: Practice safe habits like shoulder checks until they are automatic, so your attention is free for the road. Remember: habits free your attention.

audio_scripts.must_match_card_back: Practice with intent so that safe habits, such as looking over your shoulder to check blind zones, become automatic and free your attention for the changing road.

question.text: How can a cold, a headache or stress affect your driving?

answer.text: Driving demands physical and mental fitness: a bad cold can slow your thinking, a headache or tight shoulders can hurt your handling, and stress can weaken your decisions, so ask a doctor about any condition that worries you.

teaching.text: A cold, a headache or stress can hurt thinking, handling and decisions, so ask a doctor about worrying conditions. Remember: fitness affects driving.

audio_scripts.must_match_card_back: Driving demands physical and mental fitness: a bad cold can slow your thinking, a headache or tight shoulders can hurt your handling, and stress can weaken your decisions, so ask a doctor about any condition that worries you.

question.text: What should you do before starting the engine if you feel unwell?

answer.text: Check in with yourself before you start the engine, and if you feel unwell but still need to travel, have someone else do the driving.

teaching.text: Check yourself before you start, and if you feel unwell but must travel, let someone else drive. Remember: unwell? someone else drives.

audio_scripts.must_match_card_back: Check in with yourself before you start the engine, and if you feel unwell but still need to travel, have someone else do the driving.

question.text: What must you pass before Washington issues a driver license?

answer.text: Washington law requires you to pass a vision test before you are issued a driver license.

teaching.text: Washington requires a vision test before it issues a driver license. Remember: vision test first.

audio_scripts.must_match_card_back: Washington law requires you to pass a vision test before you are issued a driver license.

question.text: What are the rules for corrective lenses while driving?

answer.text: If your license requires corrective lenses, wear them every time you drive, and do not use dark or tinted corrective lenses after dark.

teaching.text: Wear required corrective lenses every drive, but not dark or tinted ones after dark. Remember: lenses always, no tint night.

audio_scripts.must_match_card_back: If your license requires corrective lenses, wear them every time you drive, and do not use dark or tinted corrective lenses after dark.

question.text: Which lenses must you wear, and which avoid at night?

answer.text: Wearing required corrective lenses is a must on every drive, but dark or tinted corrective lenses are the ones to avoid at night.

teaching.text: Required lenses go on every drive; tinted ones stay off at night. Remember: required yes, tinted no.

audio_scripts.must_match_card_back: Wearing required corrective lenses is a must on every drive, but dark or tinted corrective lenses are the ones to avoid at night.

question.text: What does peripheral vision let you do?

answer.text: Peripheral vision lets you notice vehicles and trouble from the corner of your eye while still looking ahead, and clear sight also lets you judge how far away other vehicles, people and hazards are.

teaching.text: Peripheral vision catches trouble from the corner of your eye, and clear sight judges distances. Remember: see from the corners.

audio_scripts.must_match_card_back: Peripheral vision lets you notice vehicles and trouble from the corner of your eye while still looking ahead, and clear sight also lets you judge how far away other vehicles, people and hazards are.

question.text: How do you handle night driving if it is hard for you?

answer.text: If night driving is hard for you, drive at night only when needed, keep your headlights on, and escape oncoming glare by looking toward the right edge of the road and steering by it.

teaching.text: If night driving is hard, drive at night only when needed and look to the right edge to escape glare. Remember: look right, beat glare.

audio_scripts.must_match_card_back: If night driving is hard for you, drive at night only when needed, keep your headlights on, and escape oncoming glare by looking toward the right edge of the road and steering by it.

question.text: How should you adjust your driving at night?

answer.text: At night, keep headlights properly aimed, slow down and leave more following distance, so that you can stop within the stretch of road your headlights light up.

teaching.text: At night, aim your headlights, slow down and leave more space so you can stop within their light. Remember: stop within your lights.

audio_scripts.must_match_card_back: At night, keep headlights properly aimed, slow down and leave more following distance, so that you can stop within the stretch of road your headlights light up.

question.text: How do you handle glare versus seeing farther at night?

answer.text: To handle oncoming glare you look to the right edge of the road, while to see farther you keep headlights aimed and slow down so you can stop inside their beam.

teaching.text: Look right to handle glare; aim your lights and slow down to see far enough. Remember: look right; slow down.

audio_scripts.must_match_card_back: To handle oncoming glare you look to the right edge of the road, while to see farther you keep headlights aimed and slow down so you can stop inside their beam.

question.text: Why does hearing matter, and how can deaf drivers adapt?

answer.text: Horns, sirens and screeching tires warn you of danger, hearing loss often creeps in slowly, and deaf or hard-of-hearing drivers can adapt by leaning more on their eyes and staying extra alert.

teaching.text: Horns, sirens and screeching tires warn of danger, and drivers with hearing loss rely more on their eyes. Remember: eyes make up for ears.

audio_scripts.must_match_card_back: Horns, sirens and screeching tires warn you of danger, hearing loss often creeps in slowly, and deaf or hard-of-hearing drivers can adapt by leaning more on their eyes and staying extra alert.

question.text: What does Washington law say about earbuds and headphones while driving?

answer.text: Driving while wearing earbuds, earphones, headphones or headsets that play sound or cancel noise is illegal, although a hands-free device in one ear is allowed if it meets WAC two hundred four-ten-forty-five.

teaching.text: Sound-playing or noise-cancelling earbuds and headphones are illegal; a compliant one-ear device is allowed. Remember: no earbuds; one-ear hands-free.

audio_scripts.must_match_card_back: Driving while wearing earbuds, earphones, headphones or headsets that play sound or cancel noise is illegal, although a hands-free device in one ear is allowed if it meets WAC two hundred four-ten-forty-five.

question.text: May a permit or intermediate driver use a hands-free phone?

answer.text: A driver holding an instruction permit or an intermediate license may not use a cell phone or any mobile electronic device while driving, not even a hands-free one.

teaching.text: Permit and intermediate drivers may not use any mobile device while driving, even hands-free. Remember: novices: no devices.

audio_scripts.must_match_card_back: A driver holding an instruction permit or an intermediate license may not use a cell phone or any mobile electronic device while driving, not even a hands-free one.

question.text: How does the one-ear device allowance differ for permit and intermediate drivers?

answer.text: Most drivers may use a hands-free device in one ear, but a driver with an instruction permit or intermediate license may not use any mobile device at all while driving.

teaching.text: Most drivers may use one compliant earpiece; permit and intermediate drivers may use no device. Remember: novices get no device.

audio_scripts.must_match_card_back: Most drivers may use a hands-free device in one ear, but a driver with an instruction permit or intermediate license may not use any mobile device at all while driving.

question.text: What does impaired driving mean?

answer.text: Impaired driving means anything, including alcohol, drugs or tiredness, that makes it hard to think clearly, react fast or control your car.

teaching.text: Impairment is anything, including alcohol, drugs or tiredness, that dulls thinking, reaction or control. Remember: anything that dulls you.

audio_scripts.must_match_card_back: Impaired driving means anything, including alcohol, drugs or tiredness, that makes it hard to think clearly, react fast or control your car.

question.text: What are the penalties for driving under the influence?

answer.text: Penalties for driving under the influence of alcohol or drugs include costly fines, higher insurance rates, a suspended or withdrawn license and possible jail, and no amount of experience makes drinking and driving safe.

teaching.text: DUI brings fines, higher insurance, license loss and possible jail, and experience never makes it safe. Remember: fines, insurance, license, jail.

audio_scripts.must_match_card_back: Penalties for driving under the influence of alcohol or drugs include costly fines, higher insurance rates, a suspended or withdrawn license and possible jail, and no amount of experience makes drinking and driving safe.

question.text: Which impairing substance is most often involved in impaired-driving crashes?

answer.text: Alcohol is the impairing substance most often involved in impaired-driving crashes, so watch for drivers acting impaired and give them plenty of room.

teaching.text: Alcohol is involved in impaired crashes most often, so give drivers acting impaired plenty of room. Remember: alcohol leads crashes.

audio_scripts.must_match_card_back: Alcohol is the impairing substance most often involved in impaired-driving crashes, so watch for drivers acting impaired and give them plenty of room.

question.text: How does alcohol affect your driving?

answer.text: Alcohol can make you drowsy, blur or narrow your vision, slow your reactions and scanning, make multitasking like lane keeping harder, and breed overconfidence that leads to risky moves.

teaching.text: Alcohol brings drowsiness, blurred or narrowed vision, slow reactions, poor lane keeping and overconfidence. Remember: alcohol slows and blurs.

audio_scripts.must_match_card_back: Alcohol can make you drowsy, blur or narrow your vision, slow your reactions and scanning, make multitasking like lane keeping harder, and breed overconfidence that leads to risky moves.

question.text: How do you avoid impaired driving?

answer.text: Never drive after using an impairing substance, never ride with a driver who has used any amount, stop friends and family from driving impaired, and arrange a sober driver ahead of time.

teaching.text: Never drive impaired or ride with an impaired driver, and plan a sober driver ahead of time. Remember: plan a sober driver.

audio_scripts.must_match_card_back: Never drive after using an impairing substance, never ride with a driver who has used any amount, stop friends and family from driving impaired, and arrange a sober driver ahead of time.

question.text: Who may legally use recreational cannabis, and is driving after it legal?

answer.text: Recreational cannabis in any form is legal for adults aged twenty-one or older, yet driving after using any cannabis is illegal at every age, and no amount of it is safe for driving.

teaching.text: Cannabis is legal for adults twenty-one and older, but driving after any cannabis is illegal at every age. Remember: never drive after cannabis.

audio_scripts.must_match_card_back: Recreational cannabis in any form is legal for adults aged twenty-one or older, yet driving after using any cannabis is illegal at every age, and no amount of it is safe for driving.

question.text: How does cannabis affect driving?

answer.text: Cannabis can reduce attention and coordination, slow reactions, weaken car handling and distance judgment, and make you drowsier.

teaching.text: Cannabis can reduce attention and coordination, slow reactions and weaken handling and distance judgment. Remember: cannabis dulls and slows.

audio_scripts.must_match_card_back: Cannabis can reduce attention and coordination, slow reactions, weaken car handling and distance judgment, and make you drowsier.

question.text: Does being old enough to use cannabis make driving after it legal?

answer.text: Being twenty-one or older makes recreational cannabis legal to use, but it never makes driving after cannabis legal, because that ban applies at every age and to any amount.

teaching.text: Legal cannabis use at twenty-one never makes driving after cannabis legal. Remember: legal to use, never drive.

audio_scripts.must_match_card_back: Being twenty-one or older makes recreational cannabis legal to use, but it never makes driving after cannabis legal, because that ban applies at every age and to any amount.

question.text: Does a drug being legal make it safe for driving?

answer.text: A drug being legal does not make it safe for driving, and impaired driving is a crime whether the drug was prescribed, bought over the counter or in a store, or is illegal.

teaching.text: A legal drug is not automatically safe, and impaired driving is a crime whatever the drug's source. Remember: legal isn't safe.

audio_scripts.must_match_card_back: A drug being legal does not make it safe for driving, and impaired driving is a crime whether the drug was prescribed, bought over the counter or in a store, or is illegal.

question.text: How can over-the-counter and prescription drugs affect driving?

answer.text: Over-the-counter remedies for colds, allergies or headaches can make you drowsy, and prescription drugs, much like alcohol, can dull reflexes, judgment, vision and alertness.

teaching.text: Cold, allergy and headache remedies can cause drowsiness, and prescriptions can dull reflexes and judgment. Remember: medicines can drowse.

audio_scripts.must_match_card_back: Over-the-counter remedies for colds, allergies or headaches can make you drowsy, and prescription drugs, much like alcohol, can dull reflexes, judgment, vision and alertness.

question.text: Does it matter whether an impairing drug was prescribed or illegal?

answer.text: Whether a drug is prescribed, bought over the counter or illegal changes nothing about impaired driving, which stays a criminal act in every case.

teaching.text: Prescribed, store-bought or illegal, impaired driving is always a crime. Remember: source doesn't matter.

audio_scripts.must_match_card_back: Whether a drug is prescribed, bought over the counter or illegal changes nothing about impaired driving, which stays a criminal act in every case.

question.text: When should you avoid driving after starting a medicine?

answer.text: Do not drive after first starting a prescription, a new medicine or a higher dose until you know how it affects you, and treat any label warning about operating heavy machinery as a warning about driving.

teaching.text: Wait to drive on a new medicine or higher dose until you know its effects, and heed machinery warnings. Remember: learn effects first.

audio_scripts.must_match_card_back: Do not drive after first starting a prescription, a new medicine or a higher dose until you know how it affects you, and treat any label warning about operating heavy machinery as a warning about driving.

question.text: What does a heavy machinery warning on a medicine also cover?

answer.text: A heavy machinery warning on a medicine label covers driving a car too, not only factory or construction equipment.

teaching.text: A heavy machinery warning on a medicine covers driving a car too. Remember: machinery includes cars.

audio_scripts.must_match_card_back: A heavy machinery warning on a medicine label covers driving a car too, not only factory or construction equipment.

question.text: What risk comes from combining a medicine with another medicine or alcohol?

answer.text: A medicine that seems harmless alone can cause severe impairment when combined with a second medicine or with alcohol, so read the warnings or ask a pharmacist first.

teaching.text: A harmless-seeming medicine can impair you badly when combined with another medicine or alcohol. Remember: combinations can impair.

audio_scripts.must_match_card_back: A medicine that seems harmless alone can cause severe impairment when combined with a second medicine or with alcohol, so read the warnings or ask a pharmacist first.

question.text: What is polydrug use, and why does it matter?

answer.text: Polydrug use, taking more than one kind of drug such as alcohol plus cannabis or medicines, can produce stronger effects than any one drug and is the most common impairment found in fatal crashes.

teaching.text: Polydrug use can hit harder than any one drug and is the most common impairment in fatal crashes. Remember: mixing drugs hits harder.

audio_scripts.must_match_card_back: Polydrug use, taking more than one kind of drug such as alcohol plus cannabis or medicines, can produce stronger effects than any one drug and is the most common impairment found in fatal crashes.

question.text: Why is polydrug use so dangerous?

answer.text: Polydrug use is about combining substances, and the combination can hit harder than any single one, which makes it the leading impairment in fatal crashes.

teaching.text: Combining substances can hit harder than any single one. Remember: combined is stronger.

audio_scripts.must_match_card_back: Polydrug use is about combining substances, and the combination can hit harder than any single one, which makes it the leading impairment in fatal crashes.

question.text: What causes fatigue, and how does it affect driving?

answer.text: Fatigue comes from physical or mental strain, repetitive tasks, illness or lack of sleep, and like alcohol it impairs your vision and judgment and can put you to sleep at the wheel.

teaching.text: Fatigue comes from strain, repetition, illness or lack of sleep, and impairs vision and judgment like alcohol. Remember: tired drives like drunk.

audio_scripts.must_match_card_back: Fatigue comes from physical or mental strain, repetitive tasks, illness or lack of sleep, and like alcohol it impairs your vision and judgment and can put you to sleep at the wheel.

question.text: What signs tell you to pull over and rest?

answer.text: Pull over and rest if you cannot recall the last few miles, blink often or have heavy eyelids, struggle to hold your head up, miss exits or signs, feel irritable, or drift, swerve, tailgate or hit rumble strips.

teaching.text: Missing miles, heavy eyelids, missed exits, irritability or drifting all mean pull over and rest. Remember: signs mean rest.

audio_scripts.must_match_card_back: Pull over and rest if you cannot recall the last few miles, blink often or have heavy eyelids, struggle to hold your head up, miss exits or signs, feel irritable, or drift, swerve, tailgate or hit rumble strips.

question.text: Which driving clues signal fatigue?

answer.text: Hitting rumble strips, drifting from the lane and tailgating are physical driving clues of fatigue, just like heavy eyelids, and each one means pull over and rest.

teaching.text: Drifting, tailgating and rumble strips are fatigue clues just like heavy eyelids. Remember: drifting means rest.

audio_scripts.must_match_card_back: Hitting rumble strips, drifting from the lane and tailgating are physical driving clues of fatigue, just like heavy eyelids, and each one means pull over and rest.

question.text: What should you do if you are alone and getting tired?

answer.text: Share the driving with another driver if you can, and if you are alone and getting tired, leave the road and take a twenty-minute nap rather than push on.

teaching.text: Share the driving, or if you are alone and tired, leave the road for a twenty-minute nap. Remember: pull off and nap.

audio_scripts.must_match_card_back: Share the driving with another driver if you can, and if you are alone and getting tired, leave the road and take a twenty-minute nap rather than push on.

question.text: How should you prepare for a long trip?

answer.text: Before a long trip, get enough sleep, since most people need seven to nine hours, and plan breaks roughly every one hundred miles or two hours.

teaching.text: Before a long trip, sleep seven to nine hours and plan breaks every hundred miles or two hours. Remember: sleep well, plan breaks.

audio_scripts.must_match_card_back: Before a long trip, get enough sleep, since most people need seven to nine hours, and plan breaks roughly every one hundred miles or two hours.

question.text: When is a nap the answer, and when is a break plan?

answer.text: The twenty-minute nap is the fix when you are already drowsy and alone, whereas stopping about every one hundred miles or two hours is the plan you make before a long trip.

teaching.text: Nap when you are already drowsy and alone; plan breaks before a long trip. Remember: nap when drowsy; plan ahead.

audio_scripts.must_match_card_back: The twenty-minute nap is the fix when you are already drowsy and alone, whereas stopping about every one hundred miles or two hours is the plan you make before a long trip.

question.text: How can anxiety change your driving?

answer.text: Feelings change behavior behind the wheel: an anxious driver may press too hard on the accelerator without noticing.

teaching.text: Feelings change driving; an anxious driver may press too hard on the accelerator without noticing. Remember: feelings move your foot.

audio_scripts.must_match_card_back: Feelings change behavior behind the wheel: an anxious driver may press too hard on the accelerator without noticing.

question.text: How can you calm down while parked?

answer.text: To calm down while parked, breathe in through your nose and out as if cooling hot soup, or count slowly from one to twenty or back from one hundred by threes.

teaching.text: To calm down while parked, breathe out as if cooling soup, or count slowly. Remember: soup breath, slow count.

audio_scripts.must_match_card_back: To calm down while parked, breathe in through your nose and out as if cooling hot soup, or count slowly from one to twenty or back from one hundred by threes.

question.text: What is aggressive driving, and what behaviors go with it?

answer.text: Aggressive driving is a traffic offense, meaning a driver purposely endangers people or property, and it is linked with speeding, tailgating, unsafe lane changes, poor signaling, ignoring traffic controls and crowding walkers or cyclists.

teaching.text: Aggressive driving means purposely endangering others, with speeding, tailgating and unsafe lane changes. Remember: purpose to endanger.

audio_scripts.must_match_card_back: Aggressive driving is a traffic offense, meaning a driver purposely endangers people or property, and it is linked with speeding, tailgating, unsafe lane changes, poor signaling, ignoring traffic controls and crowding walkers or cyclists.

question.text: What defines aggressive driving, and how is it classed?

answer.text: Aggressive driving is defined by intent, a driver purposely endangering people or property or forcing others to protect themselves, and it is classed as a traffic offense.

teaching.text: Aggressive driving is defined by intent and is a traffic offense. Remember: intent makes it aggressive.

audio_scripts.must_match_card_back: Aggressive driving is defined by intent, a driver purposely endangering people or property or forcing others to protect themselves, and it is classed as a traffic offense.

question.text: What penalties come with street racing and street demonstrations?

answer.text: Street racing and unauthorized street demonstrations carry severe penalties, including fines, jail and vehicle impound, for drivers and for anyone who instigates or helps.

teaching.text: Street racing and street demonstrations bring fines, jail and impound for drivers and helpers alike. Remember: racers and helpers pay.

audio_scripts.must_match_card_back: Street racing and unauthorized street demonstrations carry severe penalties, including fines, jail and vehicle impound, for drivers and for anyone who instigates or helps.

question.text: What is road rage?

answer.text: Road rage is a criminal offense: an angry reaction to a road event that turns into violence using a vehicle or another weapon, often fed by stress, tight schedules or traffic.

teaching.text: Road rage is anger at a road event that turns violent with a vehicle or weapon. Remember: anger turned violent.

audio_scripts.must_match_card_back: Road rage is a criminal offense: an angry reaction to a road event that turns into violence using a vehicle or another weapon, often fed by stress, tight schedules or traffic.

question.text: Why is road rage a criminal offense?

answer.text: Road rage is classed as a criminal offense because the anger turns into violent behavior with a vehicle or another weapon, and it can involve a passenger as well as a driver.

teaching.text: Road rage is criminal because the anger turns violent, and it can involve a passenger. Remember: violence makes it criminal.

audio_scripts.must_match_card_back: Road rage is classed as a criminal offense because the anger turns into violent behavior with a vehicle or another weapon, and it can involve a passenger as well as a driver.

question.text: What signs suggest you may be in road rage?

answer.text: Signs you may be in road rage include violent thoughts toward others, speeding up to beat a light, weaving, overusing the horn or high beams, and braking or slowing down to punish another driver.

teaching.text: Violent thoughts, weaving, horn or high-beam abuse, or braking to punish someone are road rage signs. Remember: punishing drivers is rage.

audio_scripts.must_match_card_back: Signs you may be in road rage include violent thoughts toward others, speeding up to beat a light, weaving, overusing the horn or high beams, and braking or slowing down to punish another driver.

question.text: What do you do if another driver targets you with road rage?

answer.text: If another driver targets you with road rage, move out of the way, skip honking or gestures, keep your eyes on the road, and drive to a busy place with open businesses, calling police if needed.

teaching.text: If targeted by road rage, move away, skip gestures, keep your eyes forward and drive somewhere busy. Remember: move away, find people.

audio_scripts.must_match_card_back: If another driver targets you with road rage, move out of the way, skip honking or gestures, keep your eyes on the road, and drive to a busy place with open businesses, calling police if needed.
